narrative:
# EOD Macro-Risk Brief | 2026-10-16

**Macro risk overall stands High, with 8 stories at High or above.**

**Changed Stories:**

• **France / eurozone fragility** moved to Elevated (was 5, now 6). OAT-Bund 10y spread widened to 1.0076% from 0.82%, crossing into band 2, signalling renewed sovereign-credit tension in the eurozone periphery.

• **Clearinghouses (financial chokepoint)** moved to Moderate (was 5, now 4). Treasury volatility (MOVE) fell to 98.96 from 105.87, dropping from band 1 to band 0, reducing margin-call pressure at central counterparties.

**Watch closest:** Private credit's opaque expansion remains High—largest unregulated leverage pool with limited transparency into redemption stress or counterparty concentration.

stories.name: Treasury basis trade (hidden leverage)

indicators.label: SOFR minus EFFR (%)
MOVE index (Treasury volatility)
SEC central clearing on track (0 ok / 1 slipping / 2 delayed)

stories.summary: Hedge funds run a highly leveraged arbitrage between Treasury cash bonds and futures. It is a major source of liquidity, but a spike in funding costs or Treasury volatility can force rapid unwinds, as briefly happened in March 2020 and again in 2025.

stories.name: Japan fiscal / JGB / carry trade

indicators.label: USD/JPY (yen strengthening = lower = risk)
30-year JGB yield (%)
Takaichi plan financing clarity (0 ok / 1 unclear / 2 disorderly)

stories.summary: Decades of near-zero rates made Japan the funding leg of a vast global carry trade. As the BoJ normalizes and JGB yields rise, fiscal financing gets harder and carry unwinds can transmit stress worldwide - the August 2024 mini-crash was a preview.

stories.name: Private credit's opaque expansion

indicators.label: US high-yield OAS (%, ≈310bps)
Direct-lending default rate (%, Fitch incl. distressed exchanges)
Large-fund redemption gates (0 none / 1 isolated / 2 widespread)

stories.summary: Lending has migrated from banks to lightly regulated private-credit funds, where assets are marked infrequently and leverage is opaque. Defaults are rising from a low base; the risk is that losses surface suddenly rather than being visible in real time.

stories.name: Developing-world debt crisis

indicators.label: Broad US dollar index (FRED DTWEXBGS)
US 10y real yield (TIPS, %)
New IMF programs / missed coupons (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 cluster)

stories.summary: A strong dollar, high real rates, and heavy foreign-currency debt loads leave many developing economies vulnerable to a sudden stop. A cluster of sovereign defaults or new IMF programs would signal the slow-burn crisis turning acute.

stories.name: China's price spillover (deflation or cost-push)

indicators.label: China PPI YoY (%) - large swing either way is worse
USD/CNY (yuan depreciation = higher = risk)
New tariff/anti-dumping actions (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 escalating)

stories.summary: China's factory-gate prices spill into global goods markets in BOTH directions: years of PPI deflation exported disinflation and squeezed competitors, while a sharp 2026 reversal to positive PPI (energy/commodity cost-push) now exports input-cost pressure. Either large swing is destabilising; the indicator is scored on the size of the move, not its sign.

stories.name: Critical minerals as a weapon

indicators.label: Rare-earth export license flow (0 flowing / 1 slowing / 2 frozen)
Nov-2025 pause status (0 extended / 1 expiring / 2 lapsed)
US domestic RE producer blacklist (0 none / 1 entity-specific ban / 2 sector-wide ban)
Ex-China heavy rare-earth price premium (x China)

stories.summary: China dominates the mining and especially the processing of rare earths and critical minerals, and has shown willingness to use export licensing as leverage. Supply chains for magnets and defense inputs have little near-term substitute.

stories.name: Stablecoins & Treasury demand

indicators.label: Largest stablecoin max peg deviation (%)
Total USD stablecoin supply ($bn)
GENIUS implementation friction (0 smooth / 1 gaps / 2 problems)

stories.summary: Dollar stablecoins have become sizeable holders of short-term Treasuries, linking crypto plumbing to the funding market. A large redemption wave could force rapid T-bill selling; the GENIUS Act's implementation is the key regulatory variable.

stories.name: AI build-out circular financing

indicators.label: US investment-grade OAS (%) - big-issuer proxy
AI capex-vs-revenue gap concern (0 closing / 1 wide / 2 widening fast)
GPU-backed debt refinancing stress (0 none / 1 signs / 2 acute)

stories.summary: AI infrastructure spending vastly exceeds current AI revenue, increasingly financed with debt and circular vendor arrangements. If monetization disappoints or GPU-backed financing strains, the capex cycle could reverse sharply.

stories.name: CRE maturity wall / regional banks

indicators.label: CMBS office delinquency rate (%)
Regional-bank CRE stress (0 calm / 1 isolated / 2 cluster)

stories.summary: A wall of commercial real-estate loans - especially office - matures into higher rates and lower valuations, concentrated at regional banks. Rising delinquencies and 'extend and pretend' practices defer, rather than resolve, the losses.

stories.name: France / eurozone fragility

indicators.label: OAT-Bund 10y spread (%)
Govt stability (0 stable / 1 fragile / 2 collapse-or-snap-election)
Rating action (0 stable / 1 negative outlook / 2 downgrade)

stories.summary: France combines a wide deficit, a fragmented parliament, and recurring budget standoffs, widening its spread over Germany. Political instability or a rating downgrade would test eurozone cohesion at its second-largest economy.

stories.name: Hidden consumer debt

indicators.label: Subprime auto 60+ day delinquency (%)
US unemployment rate (%)
BNPL delinquency trend (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 spiking)

stories.summary: Beneath headline figures, subprime auto and buy-now-pay-later delinquencies are climbing, and the labor market is the swing factor. A rise in unemployment would convert stretched-but-current borrowers into defaults quickly.

stories.name: Gold / de-dollarization

indicators.label: Gold price (USD/oz)
USD share of FX reserves (%, IMF COFER)
Reserve-weaponization / settlement shift (0 none / 1 talk / 2 action)

stories.summary: Central banks are accumulating gold and building non-dollar settlement arrangements at the margin. It is a slow erosion rather than a sudden shift, but reserve 'weaponization' events can accelerate diversification away from the dollar.

stories.name: Insurance retreat

indicators.label: Insurer non-renewals / exits (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 accelerating)
US single-family mortgage delinquency (%, FRED DRSFRMACBS)
Catastrophe-loss pressure (0 normal / 1 elevated / 2 severe season)

stories.summary: Insurers are retreating from climate-exposed markets through non-renewals and exits, shifting risk onto homeowners and state backstops. Severe catastrophe seasons strain the system and feed into housing and mortgage stress.

stories.name: Pensions / demographics

indicators.label: Social Security / pension reform shock (0 none / 1 debate / 2 cuts)
Pension-fund leverage event, UK-2022 type (0 none / 1 stress / 2 blowup)
Large public-pension funded ratio (%)

stories.summary: Aging demographics and underfunded public pensions create slow fiscal pressure, while leveraged liability-driven strategies can blow up fast - as the UK gilt/LDI crisis showed in 2022. Benefit-reform fights are the political pressure valve.

stories.name: AI power & the grid bottleneck

indicators.label: Grid interconnection wait (months)
Data-center moratoria / backlash (0 none / 1 spreading / 2 widespread)
AI power-demand pressure (0 easing / 1 tight / 2 acute)

stories.summary: Data-center electricity demand is colliding with multi-year grid interconnection queues and slow capacity additions. Whether this is an acute shortfall or eases depends on the pace of AI build-out versus new supply - forecasts diverge widely.

stories.name: Copper & the electrification deficit

indicators.label: Copper price (USD/lb, COMEX HG=F)
Major mine disruptions (0 none / 1 some / 2 cluster)
Deficit timing (0 surplus / 1 balanced / 2 deficit)

stories.summary: Electrification and AI infrastructure point to structural copper deficits as demand outruns new mine supply, which takes a decade to build. Price is the live signal; mine disruptions and inventory draws would confirm tightening.

stories.name: Water - the underpriced input

indicators.label: Drought in a chip/farm hub (0 none / 1 emerging / 2 acute)
Key reservoir / basin stress (0 normal / 1 low / 2 critical)
Transboundary water dispute escalation (0 calm / 1 tense / 2 crisis)

stories.summary: Water is systematically underpriced yet essential to chip fabrication, agriculture, and power. Droughts in key hubs (Taiwan's fabs, major farming regions) and transboundary disputes can disrupt supply chains in ways markets rarely price in advance.

stories.name: Food & fertilizer fragility

indicators.label: Food-price trend (0 falling / 1 elevated / 2 spiking)
China fertilizer export curbs (0 lifted / 1 in place / 2 tightened)
Hormuz/Gulf disruption to fertilizer inputs (0 clear / 1 disrupted / 2 cut)
indicators.measured_note: Strait of Hormuz 4.1 ships/day vs 92 normal (4%). Source: International Monetary Fund, PortWatch

stories.summary: Food security depends on concentrated fertilizer supply chains - potash, phosphate, and gas-derived nitrogen - exposed to export curbs and shipping chokepoints. Curbs or input shocks feed through to prices with a lag.

stories.name: The lithography (ASML) chokepoint

indicators.label: Taiwan / cross-strait tension (0 calm / 1 elevated / 2 crisis)
Export-control escalation (0 stable / 1 tightening / 2 retaliation)
Single-point concentration (0 easing / 1 high / 2 extreme)

stories.summary: ASML is the sole maker of EUV lithography machines, with Zeiss the sole optics supplier - a single point of failure for advanced chips. Export controls, retaliation, or any disruption to this chain would ripple across the entire tech economy.

stories.name: Sea lanes & undersea cables

indicators.label: Hormuz/Red Sea status (0 open / 1 contested / 2 closed)
indicators.measured_note: Strait of Hormuz 4.1 ships/day vs 92 normal (4%); Bab el-Mandeb (Red Sea) 28.3 ships/day vs 69 normal (41%). Source: International Monetary Fund, PortWatch

indicators.label: WTI crude oil (USD/bbl, CL=F)
Undersea cable incidents (0 none / 1 threatened / 2 cut)

stories.summary: A few maritime chokepoints and undersea cables carry most global trade and data. The 2026 Hormuz/Red Sea disruptions showed how quickly closures spike energy and shipping costs; cable cuts are a parallel, under-watched vulnerability.

stories.name: Clearinghouses (financial chokepoint)

indicators.label: Equity volatility (VIX)
Treasury volatility (MOVE)
Treasury-clearing rollout stress (0 smooth / 1 friction / 2 problems)

stories.summary: Central counterparties now concentrate the system's risk by design, and Treasury central-clearing mandates will route more activity through them. In a volatility spike, procyclical margin calls can amplify stress - they are a systemic single point of failure.

items.label: Large-fund redemption gates (0 none / 1 isolated / 2 widespread)
items.rationale: The rubric threshold for WIDESPREAD is >=3 of the largest funds gating in the same quarter or combined AUM >$100B; at least 7-10 named major funds have simultaneously breached their 5% quarterly repurchase caps across Q1-Q3 2026 with combined AUM well exceeding $250B, satisfying the WIDESPREAD criterion by a large margin. Corroborating signals include: FOMC policy anchored at 3.50-3.75% (higher-for-longer), sticky CPI at 4.2%, new direct-lending issuance down ~40%, and a $14B cumulative redemption backlog reported by Bloomberg (July 2026), all consistent with structural funding stress in semi-liquid private credit vehicles.
items.fact: Per Valuation Research (Oct 2, 2026), average redemption requests across 11 of the 14 largest non-traded BDCs stood at 13.0% in Q3 2026, still well above the standard 5% quarterly cap, with named funds including Blackstone BCRED (~$79B, gated at 5% after ~10% requests per Yardeni/Bloomberg Sept 2026), Cliffwater Corporate Lending Fund (~$31B, capped at 5% after 16% requests), and Blue Owl OTIC/funds (capped at 5%, 39% requests) all actively gating in Q3; in Q2 2026 Fitch tracked 10 of 16 BDCs breaching caps on $15.6B in requests (Fitch/angelinvestorsnetwork.com, ~Aug 2026); cumulative gated AUM across BCRED, Apollo ADS, BlackRock HLEND, Ares ASIF, Cliffwater, Partners Group, Blue Owl funds exceeds $250B.

items.label: BNPL delinquency trend (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 spiking)
items.rationale: 30+ DPD rose ~18-29 bps YoY through mid-FY2026 before improving in Q4, placing it squarely in the RISING band; the <100 bps YoY move precludes Score 2, and charge-offs remain below 3% on the regulator's pay-in-four series and below 5% on Affirm's own vintage metric, consistent with Score 1.
items.fact: Affirm Q4 FY2026 Earnings Supplement (Aug 27, 2026): 30+ DPD on monthly installment loans ex-Peloton/Pay-in-X = 2.5%, down from 2.7-2.8% in prior three quarters but up ~29 bps YoY in FQ3'26 per shareholder letter; cohort net charge-offs track ~3.5% of GMV (lifetime vintage). CFPB Dec-2025 report: aggregate BNPL pay-in-four charge-off rate 1.83% in 2023 (latest official figure). Richmond Fed Feb-2026: 'no direct evidence of rising aggregate BNPL charge-off rates to date.'

items.label: CMBS office delinquency rate (%)
items.rationale: The Trepp September 2026 office CMBS delinquency rate of 12.16% is the most recent published figure and maps directly to the rubric, which calls for the latest percent reading from Trepp; this sits near cycle highs and reflects persistent maturity-default stress in the office sector.
items.fact: Trepp September 2026 CMBS office delinquency rate: 12.16%, up 16 bps from August's 12.00%; per vaquerowealth.com (Oct 6 2026) and curatedcommercial.substack.com (Oct 12 2026), both citing Trepp September 2026 data.

dissent.view: KBRA reports a higher office CMBS delinquency rate of ~12.8% (Feb-Mar 2026) due to inclusion of a broader KBRA-rated universe and different loan classification methodology

why: change rests only on non-authoritative sources

items.label: Regional-bank CRE stress (0 calm / 1 isolated / 2 cluster)
items.rationale: Within the trailing 6 months, at least 1 confirmed CRE-linked failure (Nano Banc, $736M assets, <$10bn) with a public enforcement action explicitly citing CRE concentration satisfies the ISOLATED threshold of 1-2 such failures each <$10bn plus >=1 new enforcement action/consent order citing CRE concentration. CLUSTER (2) is not warranted because credible sources do not firmly attribute >=3 in-window failures primarily to CRE exposure, and no single failure exceeded $10bn or triggered a coordinated interagency action.
items.fact: FDIC failed-bank list shows 5 US bank failures in the trailing 6 months (Apr 12-Oct 12 2026): Community Bank and Trust-West Georgia (May 1), Kentland Federal S&L (Jul 10), Small Business Bank (Jul 17), Tioga-Franklin Savings Bank (Aug 21), and Nano Banc (Sep 25, $736M assets). Of these, Nano Banc is explicitly CRE-linked: American Banker (Sep 26 2026) reports it 'had been the subject of enforcement actions in connection with both commercial real estate lending and governance issues'; FedFis notes 'high concentrations in CRE'; a March 2026 DFPI consent order cited deteriorating financial condition tied to CRE concentration. Metropolitan Capital (Jan 30, CRE skilled-nursing loan) falls outside the 6-month window. No other in-window failure has explicit primary-source CRE attribution. No single failure exceeded $10bn assets; no coordinated interagency CRE supervisory action found. Source: fdic.gov/bank-failures/failed-bank-list (Oct 2026); americanbanker.com (Sep 28 2026); fintechcowboys.com/bank-failure-alert-nano-banc.

items.label: USD share of FX reserves (%, IMF COFER)
items.rationale: The IMF COFER release dated 30-Sep-2026 is the most recent official publication; it reports 56.70% as the USD share for end-June 2026 (2026Q2), which maps directly and mechanically to the rubric requiring the latest published percent figure.
items.fact: IMF COFER data brief published 30 September 2026 (data.imf.org): 'the dollar\'s share of global foreign exchange reserves declined to 56.70 percent' in 2026Q2, from 57.18 percent in 2026Q1. Total global FX reserves rose to $13.22 trillion. Source: https://data.imf.org/en/news/imf%20data%20brief%20september%2030

items.label: New tariff/anti-dumping actions (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 escalating)
items.rationale: Six or more new measures in the trailing 3 months satisfies the rubric threshold of >=4 new measures for ESCALATING (score 2), and the EU tyre anti-dumping (up to 45.3%) qualifies as a broad tariff round exceeding 10% across a sector. The ongoing US-China truce extension prevents a clean 'truce breakdown' characterization, but the measure count and sectoral breadth independently clear the ESCALATING bar.
items.fact: At least 6 distinct new major-economy trade measures against Chinese exports were enacted in the trailing 3 months: (1) EU definitive anti-dumping on Chinese car/lorry tyres (4.3%-45.3%), published July 7, 2026 (policy.trade.ec.europa.eu); (2) EU definitive anti-dumping on Chinese polyamide filament yarns (60%-67.6%), EU Reg. 2026/1823, July 27, 2026 (catts.eu/august-2026); (3) EU provisional anti-dumping on Chinese benzyl alcohol, July 27, 2026 (catts.eu/august-2026); (4) Canada CBSA provisional anti-dumping/CVD on unarmored building cables from China, effective July 29, 2026 (catts.eu/august-2026); (5) China extended anti-dumping on single-mode optical fiber from India, effective August 14, 2026 (catts.eu/august-2026); (6) US imposed 7.5% overcapacity tariff on China restoring ~20% total rate, reported August 24, 2026 (china-briefing.com). Simultaneously, the US-China bilateral truce was extended two months on September 27, 2026 (rvia.org), and US-China recommended $30bn in mutual tariff cuts (euronews.com, September 28, 2026). EU safeguard tariffs on Chinese hybrid EVs are under active deliberation but not yet enacted (asiatimes.com, October 9, 2026).

items.label: Nov-2025 pause status (0 extended / 1 expiring / 2 lapsed)
items.rationale: The truce is formally extended (not lapsed), ruling out Score 2; but partial breaches — new entity-list additions targeting the two lead US rare-earth firms and persistent sub-commitment supply volumes — satisfy the rubric's 'partial breach' prong for Score 1 (EXPIRING/fraying), and the extended deadline of Jan 10 2027 is itself <90 days from today with no further renewal announced.
items.fact: US Treasury Secretary Bessent announced on Sep 23, 2026 an extension of the Busan truce from Nov 10, 2026 to Jan 10, 2027 (Investing.com/NBC News, Sep 23 2026); however, China added MP Materials and USA Rare Earth to its export control entity list on Jun 22, 2026 (The Conversation/Modern Diplomacy), and US officials assessed Chinese rare-earth compliance at ~two-thirds of commitments with yttrium exports down ~95% (startupfortune.com, Oct 10 2026).

dissent.view: Some sources (startupfortune.com, Oct 6 2026) framed the Nov 10 date as expiring 'with no renewal in sight' before the Sep 23 extension was announced; post-extension reporting broadly converges on Jan 10 2027 as the new deadline, so the 'no renewal' characterisation is outdated but circulates in older articles.

why: change rests only on non-authoritative sources

items.label: Undersea cable incidents (0 none / 1 threatened / 2 cut)
items.rationale: The Sept 2025 Red Sea multi-cable cut is the most recent confirmed severing event but ~13 months elapsed and prior cuts of similar scale were repaired within weeks-to-months, so current severed status is unconfirmed; Iran Hormuz threats and ongoing Baltic hybrid-warfare pattern constitute credible ongoing threats, mapping to rubric level 1 (THREATENED) rather than 2 (CUT), as no market-corroborated unrepaired outage is confirmed for October 2026.
items.fact: On 6 September 2025, at least four Red Sea cables (SMW4, IMEWE, FALCON GCX, Europe India Gateway) were severed near Jeddah by likely commercial anchor drag, causing internet degradation across India, Pakistan, Gulf states and Africa (Capacity Global / Gulf News, Sept 2025). PEACE and AAE-1 cuts from early 2025 were repaired by April 2025. No confirmed new Red Sea, Baltic, or Hormuz cut is reported in 2026; Iran issued credible Hormuz cable-cut threats (Asia Times, Sept 2026) and Baltic incidents remain under hybrid-warfare investigation but no unrepaired severance confirmed.

dissent.view: September 2025 Red Sea cuts to SMW4/IMEWE/FALCON/EIG may still be unrepaired given repair-ship scarcity and geopolitical permitting delays in Red Sea conflict zone
Iran threat to cut Hormuz cables assessed as operationally feasible and affecting project planning, implying elevated risk beyond mere threat

why: change rests only on non-authoritative sources

items.label: Drought in a chip/farm hub (0 none / 1 emerging / 2 acute)
items.rationale: A confirmed government water-rationing order affecting chipmaking hubs Hsinchu and Taichung satisfies rubric level 2 ('confirmed production curtailment / water-rationing order at a fab'). The US Southwest concurrently improved to D0-D1 after tropical moisture (USDM Oct 8, 2026), so Taiwan is the binding region driving the score.
items.fact: Taiwan's Water Resources Agency imposed formal water rationing after 'the driest winter in 75 years,' with reservoirs in chipmaking hub Hsinchu County at 60-80% of 2021 severe-drought levels and Zengwen Reservoir at 28.5% capacity; private industries cut usage up to 7%. Source: Taipei Times, 2026-03-27 (https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/front/archives/2026/03/27/2003854549). By Aug-Oct 2026 southern Taiwan reservoir levels improved with rainfall (Astute Group, ~Aug 2026), but TSMC CEO still cited water as a production-planning concern in June 2026.

dissent.view: By ~August 2026, recent rainfall improved southern Taiwan reservoir levels, reducing immediate pressure on industrial water supplies — suggesting conditions may have retreated from acute to emerging by Q4 2026.

items.label: Major mine disruptions (0 none / 1 some / 2 cluster)
items.rationale: Three named top-20 mines (Grasberg, Kamoa-Kakula, Centinela) have confirmed, physically measured production cuts currently active, satisfying the >=3 threshold; additionally, multiple institutions (Goldman Sachs, BMI) have explicitly forecast a market deficit attributable to these combined losses, satisfying both prongs of the rubric's level-2 definition.
items.fact: Three confirmed major-mine disruptions active simultaneously: (1) Grasberg Block Cave (world #2) running at ~60% of capacity during phased ramp-up following Sep 2025 mud rush, with 2026 output ~35% below pre-incident forecast per Freeport 10-Q filed 2026; (2) Kamoa-Kakula (top-5 globally) 2026 guidance cut from 420,000 t to 290,000-330,000 t after 2025 seismic/flood event plus a 56-day smelter shutdown in Q2 2026 (mining.com, April 1 2026; Ivanhoe Q2 2026 release); (3) Antofagasta Centinela strike by 709 workers since Oct 7 2026, mining/haulage/development disrupted with unions projecting ~50% output cut in November (northernminer.com, discoveryalert.com, Oct 8-12 2026). BMI revised 2026 copper deficit from 72,000 t to 400,000 t citing these disruptions; Cochilco forecasts 5.27 Mt Chilean output, lowest since 2003 (discoveryalert.com, Oct 12 2026).

items.label: Direct-lending default rate (%, Fitch incl. distressed exchanges)
items.rationale: The 6.3% Fitch TTM print (August 2026) is the load-bearing fact under the rubric: it uses Fitch's broad definition inclusive of distressed exchanges and maturity extensions, is a fresh record above the April 2026 prior record of 6.0%, and no newer Fitch monthly print is publicly available as of 2026-10-12. The escalating trajectory — 5.7% Q1 → 6.0% Q2/April-May → 6.1% July → 6.3% August — corroborates sustained and worsening funding stress in private credit, consistent with elevated PIK-loan reliance and dealer-balance-sheet sensitivity to middle-market credit deterioration.
items.fact: Fitch Ratings reported the trailing 12-month US private credit default rate (across ~1,300 borrowers, inclusive of distressed exchanges and liability-management exercises) rose to a record 6.3% at end-August 2026, up from 6.1% in July; Fitch also recorded the highest monthly default event total in the prior 12 months (14 events in August). Source: Bloomberg citing Fitch Ratings report, September 14 2026 (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-14/us-private-credit-default-rate-hits-a-record-of-6-3-fitch-says); corroborated by Investment Executive, September 14 2026 (https://www.investmentexecutive.com/news/research-and-markets/u-s-private-credit-defaults-rise-fitch-4/).

dissent.view: Proskauer Private Credit Default Index: 2.51% for Q2 2026 (counts payment and financial-covenant defaults only, excludes maturity extensions)
KBRA Middle Market Default Monitor by count: 3.3% for twelve months to 30 June 2026 (adds imminent defaults and interventions)
KBRA Middle Market Default Monitor by debt: 2.4% for twelve months to 30 June 2026 (dollar-weighted)
Moody's private credit estimate: 1.6%-4.7% range for full-year 2025 (range depends on whether distressed exchanges are counted)

items.label: GENIUS implementation friction (0 smooth / 1 gaps / 2 problems)
items.rationale: The rubric scores 2 = PROBLEMS when the deadline is missed without final rules; every primary regulator missed the July 18, 2026 statutory deadline and no final implementing rule has been published as of the research date, satisfying the rubric condition unambiguously. There is no court stay or compliance-failure event, but the plain deadline miss with zero finalized rules is sufficient for a 2 rating.
items.fact: The GENIUS Act Section 13 rulemaking deadline of July 18, 2026 passed with zero final rules published by any primary federal regulator (OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC, NCUA, Treasury/FinCEN/OFAC). As of October 2, 2026, 13+ NPRMs and one interim final rule had been issued but none finalized; the Federal Reserve only issued its NPRM on September 24, 2026 with comments open until November 30, 2026; the OCC is targeting a final rule by November 2026. Sources: regwatch.io tracker (2 Oct 2026), federalregister.gov 2026-19860 (Fed NPRM, 29 Sep 2026), frame.xyz/insights/genius-act-final-rules (18 Jul 2026), Freshfields (25 Aug 2026), PYMNTS (20 Aug 2026).

dissent.view: Paradigm GENIUS Act Rulemaking Tracker shows '0/25 Final Rule completed' as of ~Oct 2026, consistent with a deadline miss but frames agency misses as common and without formal penalty, implying limited systemic consequence.

toku.com (4 Aug 2026) characterizes the miss as 'not a scandal and not unusual' given multi-agency coordination complexity, suggesting the practical impact is mitigated by the January 2027 effective date backstop.

items.label: SEC central clearing on track (0 ok / 1 slipping / 2 delayed)
items.rationale: One official 12-month extension was formally granted (Feb 2025), satisfying the rubric's score-1 criterion of 'an official extension granted.' No second extension has been announced and the first deadline has not yet passed, so rubric score 2 is not triggered.
items.fact: On Feb 25, 2025 the SEC formally extended compliance dates by one year (90 FR 11134, eff. Mar 4 2025): cash from Dec 31 2025 to Dec 31 2026; repo from Jun 30 2026 to Jun 30 2027. As of Sep 22 2026, Acting Chair Uyeda stated at the 2026 U.S. Treasury Market Conference that 'the SEC does not currently intend to extend these deadlines' (sec.gov, Sept 22 2026). No second extension has been announced; the Dec 31 2026 cash deadline has not yet passed.

dissent.view: ICI submitted a letter to Acting Chair Uyeda in Feb 2025 requesting a further extension of at least 24 months (to at least Jun 30 2028) for Treasury repo clearing; if granted this would push to score 2, but SEC has publicly refused further extension as of Sep 2026.

TBAC (May 2026) noted 'it is possible that clearing will not be available to all participants in all regions by the deadline,' signaling readiness risk but stopping short of characterizing a second delay.

items.label: Takaichi plan financing clarity (0 ok / 1 unclear / 2 disorderly)
items.rationale: Auctions are clearing well (BTC 3.76, well above rubric threshold of 3), ruling out a score of 2. However, 10y yields are at 30-year highs on persistent fiscal concern and the full funding path for Takaichi's stimulus programme remains credibly unspecified per market analysts, satisfying the rubric's UNCLEAR condition of 'funding path unspecified OR yield up >25bps on fiscal news but auctions still clearing.'
items.fact: 10y JGB auction on Oct 6 2026 cleared with bid-to-cover of 3.76 (MOF/Bloomberg, Oct 6 2026); 10y yield held ~3.02-3.12% in early October, up ~132bps YoY and ~10bps in the past month, near 30-year highs. Takaichi pledged in her Oct 5 Diet address that fiscal measures would be funded without new bond issuance, but Nomura economists noted the rhetoric 'does not necessarily mean policy will actually be adjusted.' Supplementary budget earlier in 2026 included new deficit bonds (MarketScreener). No failed auction or BOJ emergency operation reported.

dissent.view: Finobird/TradingEconomics characterise the higher auction yield (3.101% vs prior 2.995%) as signalling 'softer investor demand,' implying more stress than the strong BTC ratio suggests

MUFG Research forecast range of 2.90-3.30% for 10y JGB and notes concerns about BOJ falling behind the curve as main driver, not a discrete fiscal shock, suggesting gradual drift rather than UNCLEAR event

items.label: Treasury-clearing rollout stress (0 smooth / 1 friction / 2 problems)
items.rationale: Overall confidence (86%) clears the rubric 60% threshold and no deadline has been extended, ruling out score 2; but pending exemptive relief on inter-affiliate/extraterritorial scoping, widespread legal/documentation backlogs (88% of delayed firms), and 45% still lacking regulatory clarity squarely match the rubric definition of FRICTION (score 1). No corroborating SOFR-EFFR or repo spread stress prevents escalation to score 2.
items.fact: SIFMA/DTCC/BNY/Broadridge Pulse Survey (conducted June 2026, published Sept 22 2026): 86% of 340 respondents at least somewhat confident of meeting the mandate; however 45% still need more regulatory clarity, 88% of delayed programs cite legal/contract negotiation, and TBAC (May 2026) flagged two unresolved scoping issues (inter-affiliate exemptions, extraterritoriality) requiring pending SEC exemptive relief. No deadline extension issued; SEC reaffirmed Dec 31 2026 cash deadline (March 2026). Source: sifma.org press release Sept 22 2026; home.treasury.gov/system/files/221/TBACCharge1Q22026.pdf

dissent.view: DTCC FICC membership survey (Jul 27 2026) characterises industry as broadly ready for cash deadline with most firms 'already operationally ready' and >$1.2T daily already clearing, implying closer to score 0 for cash leg

items.label: AI capex-vs-revenue gap concern (0 closing / 1 wide / 2 widening fast)
items.rationale: Capex growth (~77–100% YoY aggregate) materially exceeds AI-attributable cloud revenue growth (~37–82% YoY), placing the gap firmly 'WIDE'; however, AI revenue is still strongly accelerating YoY across all four hyperscalers with no guidance cuts, so rubric score 1 applies rather than 2.
items.fact: Combined hyperscaler 2026 capex guided ~$725B, up ~77% YoY (vs ~$410B in 2025); Microsoft FY26Q3 capex $30.9B–$34.9B up ~85% YoY with AI revenue run rate $37B +123% YoY; Google Cloud Q2 2026 +82% YoY; AWS Q2 2026 +37% YoY (fastest in 18 quarters); Amazon raised 2026 capex to ~$220B; Alphabet to $195–205B; Microsoft to ~$190B. items.label: Catastrophe-loss pressure (0 normal / 1 elevated / 2 severe season)
items.rationale: YTD insured losses are below the 10-year average through H1 and the only hurricane of the season (Isaias) is tracking to sub-$10bn insured losses; both conditions required for NORMAL (0) are met - YTD <= 10y average and no single event >$10bn.

No single 2026 event has exceeded USD 10bn insured. YTD total remains below the 10-year average.

items.label: GPU-backed debt refinancing stress (0 none / 1 signs / 2 acute)
items.rationale: Banks offloading AI/data-center debt at a discount and Oracle facing a sustained $38B syndication wall — with an S&P downgrade to BBB- and CDS at 15-year wides — squarely satisfies Rubric-1 ('banks offloading AI/data-center debt at a discount, a named borrower facing a refinancing wall, or a rating watch on GPU-backed paper'). items.fact: JPMorgan, MUFG and co-lenders have spent 6+ months failing to fully distribute $38B in Oracle-leased data center construction debt (Texas/Wisconsin); some banks are now selling pieces at a discount to non-bank buyers. S&P cut Oracle to BBB- in July 2026; Oracle 5-yr CDS ~151 bps in early Oct 2026 (widest since 2009). Separately, ~$18B in Oracle-leased New Mexico loans quoted at 89-91 cents. No confirmed default or distressed exchange reported. Sources: Bloomberg/FT cited by Startup Fortune (Oct 11 2026), Archynewsy (Oct 11 2026), DisruptionBanking (Sep 24 2026).

items.label: Insurer non-renewals / exits (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 accelerating)

items.fact: Foster (2026) documented elevated nonrenewal rates in 13 states (many Midwest + CA/FL/LA); Weiss Ratings (Sep 8, 2026) named Utah the new nonrenewal epicenter at 4.45% of policies, ahead of CA (2.93%) and FL. items.label: Subprime auto 60+ day delinquency (%)
items.rationale: The rubric requires the latest reported Fitch subprime ABS 60+ day delinquency percent; July 2026 at 6.13% is the most recent monthly Fitch index figure surfaced, consistent with the documented seasonal second-half deterioration pattern. items.fact: Fitch Auto ABS subprime 60+ day delinquency index reversed course to 6.13% in July 2026, up from 5.80% in June 2026, per cucollector.com citing Fitch data (published ~Sept 2026). items.label: Govt stability (0 stable / 1 fragile / 2 collapse-or-snap-election)
items.rationale: France operates under a hung parliament with an explicit minority-coalition status; the government has governed only by deploying Art. 49.3 and surviving successive no-confidence votes without ever holding a working majority — the textbook definition of rubric band 1 (FRAGILE). No collapse, resignation, or dissolution has occurred.
items.fact: The Second Lecornu government (formed 10 Oct 2025) is the incumbent minority government of France. It has survived multiple no-confidence votes (most recently 2 Feb 2026, when two motions fell short of the 289-vote threshold), invoked Article 49.3 repeatedly to pass the 2026 budget, and PM Lecornu remains in office as of 9-10 Oct 2026. Sources: Wikipedia 'Second Lecornu government'; Euronews 02 Feb 2026; Al Jazeera 02 Feb 2026; JPost 09 Oct 2026.

items.label: Large public-pension funded ratio (%)
items.rationale: The Milliman PPFI is the standard monthly tracker for the 100 largest U.S. public pensions; 88.2% maps directly to the rubric as the representative funded ratio. Equable Institute's broader 253-plan universe yields 85.0% for FY2026, a materially different reading recorded in dissent.
items.fact: Milliman 100 Public Pension Funding Index (PPFI) funded ratio: 88.2% as of July 31, 2026, covering the 100 largest U.S. public defined benefit plans. items.label: New IMF programs / missed coupons (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 cluster)
items.rationale: Zero Board-approved new IMF nonprecautionary lending arrangements and zero missed coupons or defaults are confirmed in the Apr-Oct 2026 window; pipeline staff-level agreements (Senegal, Guinea) and the Yemen SMP are 'talk' not 'action' under the rubric, so the count is 0, mapping to CALM.

items.label: Pension-fund leverage event, UK-2022 type (0 none / 1 stress / 2 blowup)
items.rationale: Multiple FPC records through September 2026 explicitly characterise the LDI sector as resilient with adequate buffers; the March 2026 gilt selloff produced only limited, manageable cash calls and no forced selling or central-bank intervention. This maps cleanly to rubric band 0 (buffers adequate, no margin stress).

items.label: Rating action (0 stable / 1 negative outlook / 2 downgrade)

items.fact: S&P downgraded France from AA- to A+ on 18 Oct 2025 (within trailing 12 months); Fitch had cut AA- to A+ on 12 Sep 2025; Moody's affirmed Aa3 but moved outlook to Negative on 24 Oct 2025, reaffirmed 10 Apr 2026. items.label: Social Security / pension reform shock (0 none / 1 debate / 2 cuts)
items.rationale: The trustees report worsened the OASI depletion date by one quarter and meaningfully enlarged the long-term deficit, and reform legislation is actively debated in Congress -- satisfying rubric band 1. No cut has been legislated or automatically triggered, so band 2 is not met.

items.label: Hormuz/Red Sea status (0 open / 1 contested / 2 closed)

A top Iranian official on Oct 12 called the US response to its Hormuz reopening proposal 'inadequate', leaving no functioning diplomatic resolution in place. (Sources: straits.live live tracker 12 Oct 2026; IMF PortWatch Oct 4 2026; GulfNews/OilPrice.com Oct 12 2026)

items.label: Rare-earth export license flow (0 flowing / 1 slowing / 2 frozen)
items.rationale: The regime meets Rubric Level 1 on three independent grounds: (a) general licences cover only a whitelist of three named producers and their pre-cleared customers, not most export volume; (b) typical processing exceeds 30 days (60–120+ days in practice); and (c) new categories were added within the trailing 3 months (US entity-list additions including rare-earth supply-chain players in June 2026). Level 2 is not warranted because licences are actively being issued and no categorical suspension or country-wide denial is in effect.
items.fact: MOFCOM Announcement No. 18 (April 2025) — covering seven heavy/medium rare earths and derivative magnets including NdFeB and SmCo — remains fully in force and has never been suspended. General licenses exist but are limited to three named Chinese producers (JL MAG, Zhongke Sanhuan, Ningbo Yunsheng) covering only pre-vetted named customers. Per-shipment case-by-case review applies to all others, with a statutory 45-working-day target routinely exceeded at 60–120+ days in practice. In June 2026 MOFCOM added 10 US entities including MP Materials to its export-control list. Sources: cmgm.net (2026-08), blog.gettransport.com (2026-07), techtimes.com (2026-10-06), bisi.org.uk (2026-10-01).

dissent.view: BISI (Oct 2026) reports that the one-year suspension of October 2025 controls has been extended to 10 January 2027 following a Trump-Xi Washington summit, suggesting a modest easing on the extraterritorial track; however, the core April 2025 licensing regime remains unaffected by this extension.

CFR (Oct 2026) characterises China as continuing to 'squeeze supply' throughout 2026 under earlier controls, and notes Beijing never publicly announced it would suspend or remove the April 2025 measures — implying effective tightness closer to a Level 2 read in practice, though no formal suspension of licensing has been declared.

items.label: Single-point concentration (0 easing / 1 high / 2 extreme)
items.rationale: Zero operational overseas capacity at <=3nm nodes places the share outside Taiwan at effectively 0%, well below the <10% threshold for EXTREME. No operational overseas leading-edge fab exists at this node class, satisfying both conditions of rubric level 2.

Arizona Fab 21 Phase 1 produces only N4/N5; Phase 2 (N3) began equipment installation in Q3 2026 with volume production targeted for 2H 2027. Japan JASM Kumamoto Fab 1 operates only mature nodes (6-28nm). No overseas fab is in volume production at <=3nm. Source: TSMC Q1 2026 earnings call (April 16 2026), TSMC investor page (tsmc.com/english/dedicatedFoundry/manufacturing/fab_capacity), TrendForce April 2026, Focus Taiwan April 2026, supply-chain sources via BigGoFinance September 2026.

dissent.view: A Phoenix city government release (July 2026) cited by tech-insider.org projects ~30% of 2nm-and-beyond capacity in Arizona 'once expanded fabs are complete' — a forward-looking estimate, not current operational capacity.

items.label: Taiwan / cross-strait tension (0 calm / 1 elevated / 2 crisis)
items.rationale: Active PLA live-fire drills across five maritime zones, framed as a coercive response to Taiwan's National Day speech, constitute assertive military activity well above routine — matching Rubric 1 (ELEVATED). However, drills are assessed by Taiwan's own MND as coastline-proximate artillery exercises with no encirclement of Taiwan, no blockade, and no kinetic clash, keeping the reading below Rubric 2 (CRISIS).
items.fact: China's Maritime Safety Administration issued no-sail notices for five sea areas (Bohai Sea, Yellow Sea, East China Sea, South China Sea) for PLA live-fire drills running 12-17 October 2026, following President Lai Ching-te's Double Ten National Day address. Taiwan's Defence Minister Wellington Koo assessed on 12 Oct that the exercises are held near China's coastline — not around Taiwan itself — and involve only PLA artillery units; 4 PLA aircraft sorties and 6 PLAN vessels were detected operating around Taiwan as of 06:00 local time. No kinetic clash or blockade was reported. Source: Taipei Times / Focus Taiwan / Reuters (via US News) / Hong Kong Free Press, 12 Oct 2026.

dissent.view: Democrata.es and some AFP wire aggregators characterise Koo's language as condemning 'reckless' exercises and Taiwan 'preparing for the worst', implying higher alarm — but Koo simultaneously assessed drills as far from Taiwan and limited to artillery units, undercutting a crisis-level read.
US East Asian envoy Michael DeSombre said on 9 Oct 2026 that investors are 'overpricing' Taiwan conflict risk, and that both sides want to avoid conflict — consistent with a below-crisis assessment.

items.label: US domestic RE producer blacklist (0 none / 1 entity-specific ban / 2 sector-wide ban)
items.rationale: Two named US rare-earth producers (MP Materials, USA Rare Earth) are on China's MOFCOM export-control list as of 22 June 2026, satisfying rubric level 1 (entity-specific). The restriction is firm-specific, not a categorical sector-wide or class ban on all US rare-earth producers, so level 2 is not warranted.
items.fact: On 22 June 2026, China MOFCOM issued Announcement No. 23 of 2026, adding 10 US entities to its export control list; the two named US rare-earth producers are MP Materials Corp. and USA Rare Earth Inc. The restriction bans Chinese exporters and all global parties from supplying Chinese-origin dual-use items to those specific firms. Source: MOFCOM Announcement No. 23 of 2026, corroborated by Bloomberg (2026-06-22), Al Jazeera (2026-06-22), Benchmark Minerals (2026-06-22), and Morgan Lewis (2026-07-01). Benchmark Minerals explicitly notes 'the measure is entity-specific rather than a blanket restriction on rare earth exports to the US.'

items.label: AI power-demand pressure (0 easing / 1 tight / 2 acute)
items.rationale: Confirmed curtailment of data-center load under declared federal grid emergencies satisfies the rubric's Level 2 threshold exactly; multiple separate DOE 202(c) orders on both PJM and ERCOT constitute confirmed forced curtailment and declared grid emergencies, not merely warnings or forecasts. State-level power-scarcity-driven moratoria (NY, TX) add further corroboration.
items.fact: The U.S. DOE invoked Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act at least three times in 2026 to curtail data-center loads on PJM and ERCOT: (1) ERCOT emergency order 202-26-01 issued Jan 24 2026 (DOE.gov); (2) PJM emergency order issued May 18 2026 (Utility Dive, May 19 2026); (3) two PJM emergency orders in effect July 1-3 2026 during a record 168,158 MW peak, forcing data centers >=50 MW onto diesel backup within 15 minutes (electricchoice.com / techtimes.com, July 4 2026). items.label: China fertilizer export curbs (0 lifted / 1 in place / 2 tightened)
items.rationale: Active phosphate export suspension and urea volume quota with price floors are both confirmed in effect as of August-September 2026, squarely matching rubric level 1 (restrictions in place, unchanged). The last confirmed broadening occurred in March 2026, outside the trailing 3-month window from Oct 12 2026, so level 2 is not warranted.
items.fact: China's NDRC-linked phosphate export suspension (announced Dec 2025, extended March 2026 to cover additional phosphate varieties and NK blends) continues through at least end-2026; the 2026 urea export quota is set at 3.3 million tonnes with FOB price floors of $430-440/t -- a 34% cut vs 2025 actuals -- though Bloomberg (Aug 2026) reports the allowance was later revised up to ~5 Mt. Food Security Portal August 2026 update: 'phosphate stayed tight on constrained Sulphur supply and China's continuing export suspension.' (Sources: foodsecurityportal.org Aug 2026; S&P Global/Platts Dec 11 2025; fertilizerdaily.com Jul 29 2026; procurementinstitute.io; discoveryalert.com Sep 2026)

dissent.view: Bloomberg (reported via agbull.com, Aug 27 2026) indicates China's 2026 urea export allowance was expanded to ~5.0-5.5 Mt, near 2025 levels, suggesting partial normalization on nitrogen -- though phosphate restrictions remain firm.

items.label: Data-center moratoria / backlash (0 none / 1 spreading / 2 widespread)

items.label: Deficit timing (0 surplus / 1 balanced / 2 deficit)
items.rationale: A forecast surplus of +96,000t sits just outside the +/-100kt balanced band on the surplus side, mapping to rubric band 0 (SURPLUS). Confidence is medium because the margin is narrow — only ~4kt beyond the balanced threshold — and ICSG's own July 2026 monthly data showed a 51,000-tonne deficit, suggesting the full-year balance remains highly uncertain.
items.fact: ICSG April 2026 Copper Market Forecast revised the 2026 refined copper balance to a surplus of approximately 96,000 tonnes, reversing its October 2025 projection of a 150,000-tonne deficit; source: ICSG via MarketScreener/IndexBox/MiningWeekly, dated 23 April 2026.

dissent.view: ICSG preliminary monthly data showed a 51,000-tonne refined copper deficit for July 2026, suggesting the actual year-to-date trajectory may be tightening relative to the April full-year surplus forecast.

ICSG Jan-May 2026 preliminary data showed a 221,000-tonne apparent surplus (189,000t adjusted), well above the April full-year forecast of 96,000t surplus, pointing to a wider surplus than the annual projection.

items.label: Food-price trend (0 falling / 1 elevated / 2 spiking)
items.rationale: MoM rise of 1.5% is below the 5% SPIKING threshold and the 3-month gain (Jul-Sep) is ~3.7%, well below 10%; index is rising and at a post-2022 high, placing it squarely in ELEVATED (band 1).
items.fact: FAO Food Price Index averaged 136.0 points in September 2026, up 2.0 points (+1.5%) MoM from revised August and +5.8% YoY; third consecutive monthly increase and highest since November 2022. Source: FAO (fao.org/newsroom), released 2 October 2026.

items.label: Grid interconnection wait (months)
items.rationale: The load-bearing figure is the 61-month median from interconnection request to commercial operation for the 2025 in-service cohort (n=294, LBNL sheet 37), the most current published LBNL datapoint; this maps directly to the rubric requesting 'latest median grid interconnection wait in months'.
items.fact: LBNL Queued Up: 2026 Edition (data workbook updated May 2026, PDF June 2026, emp.lbl.gov/queues): median IR-to-COD for projects reaching commercial operation in 2025 was 61 months (~5.1 years), down from 63 months for the 2024 in-service cohort.

dissent.view: LBNL Queued Up 2025 Edition (data through end-2024) reported 55 months median IR-to-COD for the 2024 in-service cohort; Loopback Systems and other secondary sources citing this older edition still quote 55 months.
LBNL 2026 Edition narrative states 'well over 3 years' for IR-to-IA (not full IR-to-COD), which is a partial-stage metric not comparable to the full 61-month figure.

items.label: Hormuz/Gulf disruption to fertilizer inputs (0 clear / 1 disrupted / 2 cut)
items.rationale: The strait is rated CLOSED with throughput near zero (4 vs. 85 daily transits) and Brent above $100/bbl corroborates the closure signal; sulfur and ammonia fertilizer input flows from Gulf producers are effectively halted, satisfying both prongs of the rubric's level-2 threshold.
items.fact: IMF PortWatch recorded 4 transits on Oct 4 vs. pre-crisis baseline of 85/day; Brent at ~$103-104/bbl; Gulf sulfur shipments collapsed to 147,000 MT in June vs. 11-year floor of 730,000 MT; FAO reports 3-4 Mt/month of fertilizer trade stalled; strait effectively closed since Feb 28 2026 with ongoing vessel attacks and deadlocked negotiations (straits.live, IFPRI, FAO/openknowledge, Oct 12 2026)

items.label: Key reservoir / basin stress (0 normal / 1 low / 2 critical)
items.rationale: At 26.1% of capacity, Lake Mead is firmly below the rubric's 30% CRITICAL threshold, satisfying the level-2 criterion outright. The record-low elevation constitutes a confirmed physical impact (not merely a forecast), further anchoring the top-band classification.
items.fact: Lake Mead elevation 1,037.7 ft, storage 6,820,887 acre-feet, 26.1% of USBR active capacity (26.12M AF basis) as of Oct 11, 2026 — a record low since the reservoir first filled; per U.S. Bureau of Reclamation daily gauge data via coloradorivermonitor.com (USBR feed). Minimum power pool is 950 ft; reservoir is ~87.7 ft above that threshold.

dissent.view: lakelevelnow.com uses 28.95M AF total design capacity, yielding ~24% full — slightly lower percentage but same rubric band (CRITICAL).
reservoirbench.com cites 26,120,000 AF capacity basis and reports 26.1% full as of Oct 7, 2026 — consistent with primary reading.

items.label: Transboundary water dispute escalation (0 calm / 1 tense / 2 crisis)
items.rationale: The IWT is formally contested/suspended by one party (India) and rejected as such by the other (Pakistan), with active UN Security Council diplomacy and an international arbitral ruling — squarely a 'treaty suspended/contested with official threats exchanged' scenario. No kinetic action or confirmed physical diversion of water has been reported, so the threshold for level 2 is not met.
items.fact: India placed the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) in 'abeyance' on 23 April 2025 following the Pahalgam terror attack and continues to hold it so as of October 2026. On 31 August 2026, the Permanent Court of Arbitration (The Hague) ruled unanimously that the IWT remains fully in force and India's abeyance is legally impermissible; India rejected the ruling and the court's jurisdiction. Pakistan's Deputy PM raised the abeyance with the UN Secretary-General on 6 October 2026. No deliberate physical flow cut-off or armed clash has been documented. (Sources: pakera.pk, 11 Oct 2026; Al Jazeera, 1 Sep 2026; ISAS NUS, 28 Apr 2026)

dissent.view: Egypt-Ethiopia/GERD dispute also rates TENSE: Egypt issued 'all necessary measures' language at the UN on 26 Sep 2026 and Ethiopia is advancing three new Blue Nile dams, but no armed clash or confirmed flow cut-off occurred, so it also maps to 1 rather than 2.

India's position frames the abeyance as a sovereign security act, not a treaty violation, which could be read as treaty-functioning-under-force-majeure rather than 'contested'; however, the PCA explicitly rejected this framing.

flags.name: Redemption gates widespread, but HY spreads benign
flags.message: Large-fund redemption gates are rated WIDESPREAD (2) but high-yield spreads are benign. Broad gating usually coincides with visible credit stress; confirm the gates are systemic, not a couple of isolated funds.

s1_basis_trade.label: Hidden leverage in US government bonds
s1_basis_trade.gist: Hedge funds borrow heavily to trade US government bonds; if that trade unwinds fast it can freeze the market everyone treats as safe.

s2_japan.label: Japan's rates and the global cash carry trade
s2_japan.gist: Cheap Japanese money has funded bets worldwide for years; as Japan's interest rates rise, pulling that money home can ripple through global markets.

s3_private_credit.label: Private lending you can't see into
s3_private_credit.gist: A fast-growing pile of loans sits outside the banks with little public disclosure, so stress there is hard to spot until it is already large.

s4_dev_debt.label: Debt stress in developing countries
s4_dev_debt.gist: Many poorer nations owe more than they can comfortably repay; a wave of defaults can spread and pull in their lenders.

s5_china_deflation.label: China's prices spilling into the world
s5_china_deflation.gist: Big swings in China's factory prices - falling or rising - get exported to everyone else as cheaper goods or higher input costs.

s6_rare_earths.label: Rare-earth minerals used as a weapon
s6_rare_earths.gist: China controls most of the world's rare-earth processing and is now restricting it, squeezing US defense and high-tech manufacturing.

s7_stablecoins.label: Crypto dollars and US government debt
s7_stablecoins.gist: Stablecoins must hold US Treasuries as backing, so their rapid growth - or a sudden wobble - now feeds straight back into the government-debt market.

s8_ai_capex.label: The AI spending boom
s8_ai_capex.gist: Enormous borrowing to build AI data centers is racing ahead of the revenue meant to justify it, concentrating the risk in a few giant companies.

s9_cre.label: Commercial real estate and small banks
s9_cre.gist: Half-empty offices and loans coming due strain the regional banks that hold them - a slow-burning credit risk.

s10_france.label: France and eurozone stability
s10_france.gist: A politically gridlocked, heavily indebted France is the soft spot that could reopen broader euro-area stress.

s11_consumer_debt.label: Household debt strain
s11_consumer_debt.gist: Rising late payments on car loans and buy-now-pay-later show households stretching - an early warning on consumer health.

s12_gold_dedollar.label: Gold and moving away from the dollar
s12_gold_dedollar.gist: Central banks stockpiling gold and building non-dollar payment systems slowly chip away at the dollar's dominance.

s13_insurance.label: Insurers pulling back
s13_insurance.gist: As disaster losses climb, insurers raise prices or quit whole regions, leaving homes and assets exposed.

s14_pensions.label: Pensions and an aging population
s14_pensions.gist: Aging populations and underfunded pensions strain public budgets; leveraged pension funds can also break in a sudden rate shock, as the UK saw in 2022.

s15_ai_power.label: AI's strain on the power grid
s15_ai_power.gist: AI data centers need more electricity than the grid can quickly supply, triggering curtailments, building moratoria, and multi-year connection queues.

s16_copper.label: Copper for electrification
s16_copper.gist: Electrifying everything needs far more copper than mines can deliver, and major mine outages are tightening supply further.

s17_water.label: Water as a hidden constraint
s17_water.gist: Droughts and shrinking reservoirs threaten chip factories, farms, and power generation - an underpriced input with no substitute.

s18_food_fertilizer.label: Food and fertilizer supply
s18_food_fertilizer.gist: Export curbs and shipping disruptions to fertilizer raise the risk of higher food prices down the line.

s19_lithography.label: The chipmaking chokepoint
s19_lithography.gist: The most advanced chips depend on one Dutch tool-maker and Taiwan's factories; any disruption there hits the entire tech economy.

s20_sea_lanes.label: Shipping lanes and undersea cables
s20_sea_lanes.gist: Key straits like Hormuz and the undersea cables carrying the internet are vulnerable chokepoints for global trade and data.

s21_clearinghouses.label: The financial system's plumbing
s21_clearinghouses.gist: Clearinghouses sit at the center of every market; if one seized up under stress, it would jam trading everywhere at once.

playbook.disclaimer: Educational cause-and-effect only - how stress like this has historically moved through the system. Nothing here is investment advice or a prediction.

s1_basis_trade.mechanism: A rates shock forces highly leveraged government-bond arbitrage positions to unwind at once: margin calls trigger forced Treasury selling, liquidity in the world's benchmark market evaporates, and everything priced off it reprices.
benefits: cash and short-term bills through the panic
long-term government bonds AFTER central-bank intervention
s1_basis_trade.watch: The funding-spread and bond-volatility rows above; the historical pivot was the central bank announcing a backstop facility.
s1_basis_trade.trap: In past episodes the 'safe' asset itself fell first - forced sellers sell what they can - so the flight-to-safety instinct lost money until the intervention.

s2_japan.mechanism: Surging Japanese yields pull decades of cheap yen funding home: the yen spikes on repatriation, and leveraged positions worldwide that were financed in yen get liquidated together - hitting high-momentum equities and emerging markets hardest.
benefits: Japanese banks and insurers as rates normalize
s2_japan.watch: The 30-year JGB row above (live official feed) and the yen; past unwinds announced themselves through the currency.
s2_japan.trap: Historical carry unwinds were violent but brief - the 2024 episode round-tripped within days; the durable shift was in Japanese financials, not the panic.

s3_private_credit.mechanism: One honest markdown forces everyone's marks: investor withdrawals hit gates, gated funds fire-sell into an illiquid market, and lending to mid-sized companies contracts just as they need to refinance.
bleeds: private-credit vehicles trading below stated asset value
benefits: holders of dry powder buying discounted credit afterwards
public high-quality credit as the flight destination
s3_private_credit.watch: The default-rate and redemption-gate rows above; public high-yield spreads are the honest proxy for hidden marks.
s3_private_credit.trap: Opacity means the repricing arrives as a sudden gap, not a trend - by the time it is public, the move has largely happened.

s4_dev_debt.mechanism: A cluster of sovereign defaults - not one - overwhelms the restructuring machinery: redemptions from emerging-market debt funds force indiscriminate selling of strong and weak credits alike, and stress spreads through common creditors.
benefits: and historically the buyers of defaulted debt after restructuring - among the best-documented recoveries in fixed income
s4_dev_debt.watch: The new-IMF-programs row above and the dollar's strength, which is usually the upstream cause.
s4_dev_debt.trap: Index diversification means one or two defaults barely register; the systemic wave this story warns of is exactly what official bailouts exist to prevent.

s5_china_deflation.mechanism: Deepening factory-gate deflation is exported as cheaper goods, compressing margins for competing producers everywhere - unless Beijing's stimulus response whipsaws the pressure into a sudden commodity and China-equity rebound.
benefits: long-term bonds in the deflation leg
Chinese equities and industrial metals in the stimulus leg
s5_china_deflation.watch: The producer-price row above and any stimulus announcement - the two legs point opposite directions.
s5_china_deflation.trap: Policy whipsaw: historically every stimulus rumor violently reversed the deflation trade within days.

s6_rare_earths.mechanism: Export restrictions tighten into denial: magnet and heavy-rare-earth supply to defense, vehicle, and robotics manufacturers halts, panic stockpiling begins, and processing capacity outside China re-rates from commodity business to strategic asset.
bleeds: vehicle and defense production schedules in the short run
s6_rare_earths.watch: The license-flow, blacklist, and ex-China premium rows above - the premium is the market's own severity gauge.
s6_rare_earths.trap: Historically these moves reversed as fast as they started on any truce headline, and diversified funds in the space often hold the Chinese producers too.

s7_stablecoins.mechanism: A run on a major stablecoin forces its reserves - tens of billions in short-term government debt - to liquidate within days, briefly dislocating the bill market while the crypto ecosystem's dollar rails seize and leveraged positions cascade.
benefits: historically the surviving issuer gained lasting market share after each depeg scare
s7_stablecoins.watch: The live peg-deviation and supply rows above (updated daily from the aggregator) - past runs announced themselves in the peg first.
s7_stablecoins.trap: Crypto markets have a long history of face-ripping rebounds inside downtrends; past episodes punished conviction in both directions.

s8_ai_capex.mechanism: The debt-financed buildout meets a revenue shortfall: one credit event at a leveraged data-center operator reprices all AI-adjacent borrowing, capital-spending guidance gets cut, chip orders fall, and power-demand forecasts deflate - the whole complex moves together because it was funded together.
bleeds: power producers priced on AI demand
benefits: and - the dot-com lesson - the post-bust survivors compounded for a decade
s8_ai_capex.watch: The capex-gap, revenue-gap, and refinancing rows above; credit stress historically led equity repricing.
s8_ai_capex.trap: Bubbles run longer than solvency: betting against this one early has been the era's classic ruin trade, which is why timing signals matter more than valuation.

s9_cre.mechanism: Office refinancing failures cluster into bank failures: deposit flight spreads to lookalike regional lenders, credit to small business contracts, and commercial-property marks finally reflect reality.
benefits: the largest banks via deposit inflows
and historically the whole sector rebounded within days of a backstop
s9_cre.watch: The bank-failure and office-delinquency rows above and the official problem-bank list.
s9_cre.trap: The 2023 backstop bottomed the sector in 48 hours - the policy response, not the failure, was the historical turning point.

s10_france.mechanism: Fiscal paralysis pushes French borrowing costs through crisis thresholds: banks holding the government's own bonds absorb the losses, the sovereign-bank doom loop reawakens, and stress spreads across euro-area borrowing costs.
bleeds: other high-debt euro members through contagion
benefits: and non-euro safe havens in every euro crisis
s10_france.watch: The OAT-Bund spread row above (live feed) - it is the market's single-number verdict on this story.
s10_france.trap: The central bank: euro-breakup positioning has been ruined repeatedly by ECB backstops built precisely for this scenario.

s11_consumer_debt.mechanism: Subprime stress spreads upward: rising late payments become charge-offs, lenders tighten, discretionary spending cracks, and the weakness travels from consumer lenders to retailers to the broad economy.
benefits: trade-down retailers in every past consumer squeeze
s11_consumer_debt.watch: The subprime-delinquency and BNPL rows above; the staples-versus-discretionary ratio is the market's own recession gauge.
s11_consumer_debt.trap: Lenders provision ahead of losses - their shares historically bottomed while delinquencies were still rising.

s12_gold_dedollar.mechanism: A reserve-weaponization event accelerates the slow shift: central banks swap dollar assets for gold at a faster pace, marginal foreign demand for government debt weakens, and the metal gains a structural, price-insensitive buyer.
bleeds: long-term government bonds via lost foreign demand
benefits: gold above all - the current central-bank buying era is the live example - plus non-dollar safe havens
s12_gold_dedollar.watch: The reserve-share row above (quarterly official data) and central-bank purchase reports.
s12_gold_dedollar.trap: This is measured in decades, not events - and gold miners have historically lagged the metal itself across full cycles.

s13_insurance.mechanism: A mega-catastrophe season collides with insurers already exiting exposed regions: property becomes uninsurable, collateral values fall, and the stress transmits to mortgages, regional lenders, and state backstops.
bleeds: property values and lenders in exposed regions
benefits: historically reinsurers AFTER the event as pricing hardened
and catastrophe-linked debt yields for risk-bearers
s13_insurance.watch: The insurer-exit and catastrophe-loss rows above plus the season's forecasts.
s13_insurance.trap: Positioning before the event absorbs the loss; the well-documented historical pattern favored the post-event hard market.

s14_pensions.mechanism: A rate spike forces leveraged pension strategies into collateral calls: they dump whatever is liquid, the selling pushes yields higher still, and the spiral continues until a central bank steps in - the UK lived this in 2022.
bleeds: long-term government bonds during the spiral itself
retirees' security in the slow version
benefits: whoever provided liquidity at the intervention - the 2022 central-bank entry marked the exact bottom - and retirement insurers structurally as rates rose
s14_pensions.watch: The funded-ratio row above (live monthly feed) and long-bond volatility.
s14_pensions.trap: Identical to the basis trade: buying the falling 'safe' asset before the intervention caught knives for days.

s15_ai_power.mechanism: Data-center demand outruns the grid so badly that curtailments, connection queues, and building moratoria stall the buildout - rising household bills turn it political, and the constraint moves from engineering to consent.
bleeds: utilities caught between regulators and demand
benefits: and nuclear/gas capacity - though see the trap
s15_ai_power.watch: The interconnection-wait and moratoria rows above and capacity-auction prices.
s15_ai_power.trap: The famous version of this trade assumes the buildout CONTINUES; this story's actual blow-up - moratoria stopping it - points the opposite way for the same names.

s16_copper.mechanism: A structural deficit meets a supply shock - a major mine closure removes years of planned supply - and the metal prices high enough to ration demand, raising costs for every grid, vehicle, and data-center project simultaneously.
benefits: producing miners with volume to sell
s16_copper.watch: The mine-disruption and deficit rows above and exchange inventory levels.
s16_copper.trap: The political risk that causes the shocks sits inside the producers themselves - the closed mine may be the one you were counting on.

s17_water.mechanism: Severe drought hits a chip hub, a farm belt, and cooling-dependent power at once: an unpriced input becomes a binding constraint, cutting industrial output regionally and feeding into food prices.
benefits: historically crop prices in drought years
s17_water.watch: The reservoir and drought rows above (live official feed for the largest US reservoir).
s17_water.trap: There is no pure play - broad 'water' funds are mostly global industrials, while the shock is local; the honest effects are second-order.

s18_food_fertilizer.mechanism: Fertilizer export restrictions cut application in poorer countries, next season's yields fall, grain prices spike, and food inflation becomes social and fiscal stress in import-dependent nations - looping back into the developing-world debt story.
benefits: fertilizer producers in every past squeeze
s18_food_fertilizer.watch: The FAO food-price row above (live feed) and the export-curb indicator.
s18_food_fertilizer.trap: Fertilizer stress historically reversed violently when curbs lifted, taking back most of the move.

s19_lithography.mechanism: Conflict or blockade around Taiwan stops the fabs that make nearly all leading-edge chips: every electronics supply chain seizes within a quarter, and the shock is large enough that markets themselves may not function normally.
bleeds: and anything with a chip in it
s19_lithography.watch: The tension and export-control rows above; false-alarm cycles have historically outnumbered real escalations many times over.
s19_lithography.trap: In the true scenario, settlement and market access are themselves at risk - analysis that assumes functioning markets may not apply.

s20_sea_lanes.mechanism: A chokepoint closes - this board just watched Hormuz do it - and shipping rates, war-risk insurance, and energy prices spike together while longer reroutes quietly shrink effective global capacity; cable cuts do the same for data.
s20_sea_lanes.watch: The live strait-transit feed and cable-incident rows above.
s20_sea_lanes.trap: This board's own history shows it: reopening headlines crushed the shipping move within days - persistence of the disruption was everything.

s21_clearinghouses.mechanism: A major member defaults into a volatile market and the clearinghouse's loss waterfall activates: surviving members face assessments and de-risk simultaneously, margin requirements spiral procyclically, and the plumbing everyone assumed away becomes the crisis itself.
benefits: almost nothing leveraged - which is the honest answer; cash
and physical assets have no counterparty
s21_clearinghouses.watch: The clearing-mandate rollout row above and any clearinghouse margin announcements.
s21_clearinghouses.trap: The deepest on the board: in a true clearing failure, a winning derivative position may itself not pay out.

context.intro: The famous dials, for contrast. These are the most-watched macro gauges in the world - shown here so you can compare them with this tracker's structural lens. They are not part of the score. When they disagree with the gauge above, that divergence is the story: markets price these continuously, while the risks this tracker follows are the kind markets historically ignored until they ruptured.

items.label: VIX
items.note: Expected US stock-market volatility - the most-watched fear gauge. Calm markets usually sit below ~20.

items.label: 10y-2y curve
items.note: 10-year minus 2-year Treasury yield. A negative (inverted) reading has historically preceded US recessions - with long and variable lags.

items.label: High-yield spread
items.note: The extra yield markets demand to lend to risky companies - the market's own price of credit stress. Calm is roughly below ~4.

items.label: Chicago Fed NFCI
items.note: The Chicago Fed's broad financial-conditions index across money, debt, and equity markets. Negative = looser (calmer) than average.

items.label: Unemployment
items.note: The US unemployment rate - the classic real-economy dial, updated monthly.
